## FAIR contribution

The guide primarily supports the following FAIR principles:

**Findable**

- Software can be discovered by researchers and automated systems.
- Metadata describes what your software does.
- Persistent identifiers allow stable referencing.

**Accessible**

- Released software versions remain available over time.
- Researchers can access the information needed to obtain and use the software.

**Reusable**

- Others can identify, cite, and use specific versions of your software.

:::

# Why publish your software?

Research software is a scientific output. A workflow, analysis tool, or simulation package can represent a substantial research contribution, but only if others can discover, understand, and reuse it.

Making source code publicly available is an important first step, but a public repository alone does not guarantee that your software is findable or reusable.

For software to become part of the scientific ecosystem, researchers need to be able to:

- discover the software;
- understand its purpose;
- access a usable version;
- identify the version used in a publication;
- cite the developers who created it.

Repositories, archives, and registries help provide this context by adding metadata, persistent identifiers, and structured descriptions around your software.

# Before you start

This guide assumes that you already have:

- a source code repository (for example GitHub or GitLab);
- a README describing your software;
- an open-source license;
- a way to create software releases or versions.

A software license defines how others are allowed to use, modify, and redistribute your software. Without a license, others may be able to view your code, but they cannot easily determine what they are permitted to do with it.

If you are unsure which license fits your project, [Choose a License](https://choosealicense.com/) provides an overview of common open-source licenses and helps you select one based on your goals.

If you are still setting up the foundations of your project, see:

- [Software engineering quality](3software_engineering_quality.qmd)
- [Version control and packaging](5version_control_and_packaging.qmd)
- [Documentation](4documentation.qmd)

# Code hosting, archives, and registries

The term *repository* is often used broadly, but different platforms serve different purposes.

Understanding these differences helps you decide where your software should be published.

## Code hosting platforms

Code hosting platforms are where software is developed and maintained.

Examples include GitHub and GitLab.

They provide:

- version control;
- collaboration tools;
- issue tracking;
- code review;
- automation.

A code hosting platform answers:

> How is this software being developed?

It does not necessarily answer:

> Which version was used for a scientific result?

For that, you need software archives.

## Software archives

A software archive preserves a specific version of your software and provides a persistent reference.

This matters because software changes over time. A repository URL may point to a different version in the future than the version used in a publication.

Archiving a release allows researchers to identify the exact version of software used in an analysis.

For example:

- Version 1.0 is archived and receives a persistent identifier.
- Version 1.1 is released later and receives its own identifier.
- Both versions remain available.

## Software registries

Software registries describe software using structured metadata.

Unlike archives, registries do not primarily preserve software releases. Instead, they improve discoverability.

Researchers often search for software based on scientific questions rather than software names:

- Which tools analyse genomic variants?
- Which software supports this data format?
- Which tools are available for this biological workflow?

Registries connect these scientific needs with available software.

# Licensing and compatibility

A license determines what others are legally allowed to do with your software: use it, modify it, redistribute it, or build on it commercially. Publishing source code without a license does not place it in the public domain—by default, no one has permission to reuse it at all.

## Choosing a license

Most research software uses a permissive license, which allows almost any use with minimal restrictions:

| License | Key characteristic |
|---|---|
| MIT | Very permissive; requires only attribution |
| Apache 2.0 | Permissive; also grants an explicit patent license |
| BSD 3-Clause | Permissive; similar to MIT with an added non-endorsement clause |
| GPL-3.0 | Copyleft; derivative works must also be released under the GPL |

Permissive licenses maximise reuse, including in commercial or closed-source projects. Copyleft licenses such as the GPL guarantee that derivative works stay open, but restrict how the software can be combined with differently-licensed code.

[Choose a License](https://choosealicense.com/) walks through this trade-off and recommends a license based on your goals. The [Open Source Initiative's license list](https://opensource.org/licenses) is the authoritative reference for which licenses are recognised as genuinely open source.

## Checking compatibility with dependencies

Your license choice is not independent of the licenses of the software you depend on. Combining GPL-licensed code into your project, for example, typically requires your own project to also be released under the GPL—even if you originally intended a permissive license.

Before publishing, check the license of every dependency you rely on, particularly for:

- copyleft dependencies that may impose obligations on your own license;
- dependencies with no license at all, which cannot legally be redistributed;
- dependencies whose license restricts commercial use, if that matters for your project.
